Sheung Shui records 39.8 degrees

At 3pm and 4pm, Sheung Shui recorded 39.8 degrees, the highest temperature in Hong Kong since automatic weather stations were set up in the 1980s. At the Hong Kong Observatory, the highest temperature recorded was 36.9 degrees, the highest since records began in 1884. Yuen Long Park, Ta Kwu Ling, Happy Valley recorded 37.3 degrees, Tseung Kwan O 36.9 degrees, and Sham Shui Po 36.5 degrees.

Work warning issued based on "Hong Kong Heat Index" According to the Labour Department's guidelines, the Labour Department issues work heat stress warnings based on the "Hong Kong Heat Index" measured by the Hong Kong Observatory at King's Park. When the "Hong Kong Heat Index" reaches 30 to 32, a yellow work heat stress warning is issued, indicating that heat stress is rather high in some working environments. When it reaches 32 to 34, a red warning is issued, indicating that heat stress is very high in some working environments. The black warning is only issued when the index reaches 34, indicating that heat stress is extremely high in some working environments.

Only meets yellow warning criteria Although today's temperature broke records spanning over a hundred years, the Hong Kong Observatory's "Hong Kong Heat Index" at 3pm was only 31.3, meeting only the yellow warning criteria. The Labour Department's guidelines also point out that if other monitoring stations show that heat stress conditions at various locations in Hong Kong have reached a certain level, even if the index at King's Park has not reached that level, the Labour Department will still issue the corresponding work heat stress warning.

What is the Hong Kong Heat Index? The Hong Kong Heat Index is a heat stress index jointly developed by the Hong Kong Observatory and the CUHK Faculty of Medicine, based on the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index. It incorporates meteorological data such as ambient temperature, humidity, air flow, and solar heat radiation levels, along with overall hospital admission figures in Hong Kong for consideration.

Never seen red or black since launch?

Since the heat stress work warning was launched in 2023, red and black warnings have never been issued. According to records, from 15 May 2023 to 31 July this year, a total of 199 heat stress work warnings were issued, all yellow.

Labour Department: But relative humidity is low and wind conditions are favourable The Labour Department replied to enquiries that although today's (9th) temperature was particularly high, the relative humidity was lower than the usual summer situation, and combined with favourable wind conditions, the "Hong Kong Heat Stress Index" measured by the Observatory at ten locations today was mostly between 30 and less than 32. The Labour Department therefore issued a yellow heat stress warning based on the mechanism.

Warning issued if four out of nine monitoring stations meet criteria

The Labour Department also pointed out that the Observatory released heat index data for more districts in April this year. From 20 April, the Labour Department further enhanced the "Work Heat Stress Warning" system by incorporating heat index data from more districts as criteria for issuing "Work Heat Stress Warnings". In addition to the "Hong Kong Heat Index" data measured at King's Park, data from nine other locations has also been included as criteria for issuing "Work Heat Stress Warnings".

The Labour Department stated that if four or more of the other nine "Hong Kong Heat Index" monitoring stations show that heat stress conditions at multiple locations in Hong Kong have reached a certain level, even if the King's Park index has not reached that level, the Labour Department will still issue the corresponding "Work Heat Stress Warning". The Labour Department said it will closely monitor hot weather and the operation of the "Work Heat Stress Warning" system, and review whether the system requires further enhancement.

References temperature, humidity, air flow, and heat radiation data

The Labour Department added that the "Hong Kong Heat Index" is a heat stress index jointly developed by the Hong Kong Observatory and the CUHK Faculty of Medicine, based on the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature index. Its calculation formula is similar to the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature, incorporating meteorological data such as ambient temperature, humidity, air flow, and solar heat radiation levels, along with Hong Kong's overall hospital admission figures for consideration. It can appropriately reflect the health risks faced by the general public in Hong Kong due to heat stress.

Labour Department: Temperature is only one of the risk factors

The Labour Department emphasised that temperature is only one of the risk factors for heat stress; humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation are also factors. The Labour Department has always advocated using the "Guidelines" rather than relying solely on temperature as the criterion for assessing heat stress risks.

The Labour Department also pointed out that if an employee suffers injury or death during employment (including injury or death caused by work-related heat stress accidents), the employer must bear compensation liability. Whether a case constitutes a work injury and whether the employer must bear employee compensation liability must be considered based on the facts, specific circumstances, and objective conditions of each individual case, and cannot be generalised.
